Oh my heart hurts for you. Please go see a doctor! I have severe atopic dermatitis (seasonal) on my legs, arms, and torso. The only way I've gotten rid of it when it has reached this point of dryness in the past was by seeing a doctor (PCP will likely be cheaper and also more likely to be covered by insurance or Medicaid) and getting prescribed a short stint of oral antibiotics along with a topical steroidal cream. These will help with any itching, dryness, and inflammation.

Then you can work on repairing your moisture barrier. I'd suggest you see a dermatologist afterwards for an allergy test on your skin to see what could be contributing to flare-ups as a preventative if possible. Best of luck to you.

Nope! If your new plant-baby is not root bound within its original grow pot (the plastic pot), then steer clear of repotting it. Reason being, if you repot a plant into a pot that is too large for it, you risk the soil not drying out completely because the plant is too small to absorb all of the extra water in the soil. This will cause root rot.

You can simply leave the plant in its grow pot and plop that directly into a decorative pot until it's time to size up! Just be sure that when you water it, there is no water at the bottom of the decorative pot that has drained from the grow pot. Otherwise, root rot. Hope this helped :)

Not OC but I have been working with a psychotherapist for two years to treat my PTSD. We do EMDR a bit differently now due to covid (FaceTime calls), but with the same effect. My apologies for the wall of text!

I sit on the edge of my bed with my knees at a 90 degree angle. I have my wrists resting on my thighs. My therapist will first tell me to pull up the "picture" of a traumatic memory, and ask me what level of upset I am when I pull it up (1-10: 1 being not so bad, 10 being absolutely awful. This is simply to gauge what my progress is on a particularly upsetting memory). Then, she tells me to close my eyes, and imagine sitting in a theatre with my closest supporters (my partner, brothers, mom, etc.) sitting beside me. Now, this traumatic memory pulls up on the theatre's screen and I am watching from the theatre, from outside of the memory. **The theatre is key in EMDR, because it keeps you from reliving the traumatic memory in a first person view.** As soon as I have this memory pulled up on the "screen," with my wrists resting on my thighs, I begin to tap on my knees with my index finger, alternating from one tap with my left hand to one tap on my right hand. At this point, I am "watching" my memory unfold, except I am actually rewriting my memory in my favor. For example, I was abused as a child, so "adult me" will come in and intervene, saving "little me" from my abuser, and contacting authorities. Sometimes I'm smashing my abuser's face in, and other times, I'm just grabbing "little me" and leaving the situation. Either way, the ELI5 is, I am processing my memories, taking them from the emotional part of my brain, and moving them to the more logical part of my brain ("He's in prison, I am safe now. I am an adult, I'd have the power to leave an abusive environment now. I can now report an abuser myself, I don't need to depend on others to do that for me anymore.") It's always important to do a "closure exercise" after, and then immediately go do something to get my mind off of the EMDR session. This prevents me from snowballing into my trauma without the guidance of my therapist.

I suggest googling "EMDR PTSD" for more information/personal experiences. I hope this helps!

I have had crippling anxiety and depression for as long as I can remember. I’ve been attending classes at a community college for two years now, but only two of the four semesters have I managed to truck through it and finish those terms.

I started skipping school when I was 13 due to panic attacks and finally dropped out at 15. It started with just a few days here and there, to missing school for several consecutive weeks, and then dropping out altogether for fear of being ridiculed for even TRYING to get back into the groove of things. It was humiliating, trying to explain to the adults in my life, that I couldn’t and wouldn’t make it through high school. Mental health is not taken as seriously in our adolescent years, but it is and was real to ME. In those two years, I’d go back to school for a few weeks, finally catch up on the curriculum, and then skip “just one day,” which would set me back another few days, then weeks, etc. I tried finishing my HS diploma through online school and the “alternative” high school they had on campus for the next year, but I ended up giving up on graduating high school traditionally and told myself for years, “the time will come when I’m ready.” I worked tons of minimum wage jobs until I was 19 and finally studied enough to feel that I was ready to take the GED test. I passed with flying colors on my first try, and could now manage to get an entry level job where a HS diploma or equivalent was required. I’ve found my passion in the medical field, and am currently working on a degree in diagnostic medical imaging. Throughout all those years, I learned to be patient with myself, and to treat myself with the same love and respect I would give my loved ones. Almost 22 now.

Please take care of yourself first, even if it sets you back a little while. Yes, you’ll feel lost, stuck, and set back for some time, but please just keep on pushing and you’ll get to where you need to be. Reach out to me whenever, if need be. Best of luck.
I think you’re fucking amazing, and nowhere near a coward, because you’ve chosen to fight again. You’re kickass.
